title: Conditional Reasoning: Implications, Inference & Boolean Logic
description: Explore essential mathematical concepts through carefully crafted questions. Strengthen your understanding, practice your reasoning, and learn at your own pace.

questions.learningObjective: Apply modus ponens to draw valid conclusions from a true conditional statement.
questions.question: Consider the statement: "If it rains, then the outdoor concert is cancelled." This conditional is known to be true, and it is also known that it rains. What can be validly concluded?

options.label: C
options.text: Nothing can be concluded from the given information.

questions.explanation: This is an application of modus ponens: if \(p \rightarrow q\) is true and \(p\) is true, then \(q\) must be true. Since the conditional holds and the antecedent ("it rains") is true, the consequent ("the outdoor concert is cancelled") must also be true.
questions.hint: Think about what modus ponens allows you to conclude when both the implication and its antecedent are true.

questions.learningObjective: Apply modus tollens to draw valid conclusions from a true conditional statement.
questions.question: The conditional "If it rains, then the outdoor concert is cancelled" is true. Suppose it is observed that the outdoor concert is not cancelled. What can be validly concluded?

options.label: B
options.text: No valid conclusion can be drawn about whether it rains.

questions.explanation: This is modus tollens: if \(p \rightarrow q\) is true and \(q\) is false, then \(p\) must be false. Since \(q\) ("the outdoor concert is cancelled") is false (that is, "the outdoor concert is not cancelled"), \(p\) ("it rains") cannot be true, so it must be false — that is, "it does not rain."
questions.hint: Recall that a true implication is only violated when the antecedent is true and the consequent is false — use this to reason backward.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize that denying the antecedent does not yield a valid conclusion.
questions.question: The conditional "If it rains, then the outdoor concert is cancelled" is true. It is observed that it does not rain. What can be validly concluded about whether the outdoor concert is cancelled?

options.label: A
options.text: The outdoor concert is not cancelled.

options.label: C
options.text: It cannot be determined whether the outdoor concert is cancelled.

questions.explanation: A conditional \(p \rightarrow q\) says nothing about what happens when \(p\) is false; \(q\) may be true or false. Concluding that \(q\) is false from \(\neg p\) is the fallacy of denying the antecedent. Since "it does not rain" (the antecedent is false), the truth of "the outdoor concert is cancelled" is left undetermined by this conditional alone.
questions.hint: Check whether the implication makes any promise about the consequent when the antecedent is false.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize that affirming the consequent does not yield a valid conclusion.
questions.question: The conditional "If it rains, then the outdoor concert is cancelled" is true. It is observed that the outdoor concert is cancelled. What can be validly concluded about whether it rains?

options.label: A
options.text: It cannot be determined whether it rains.

questions.explanation: Knowing \(q\) is true does not let us conclude \(p\) is true, since \(p \rightarrow q\) allows \(q\) to be true even when \(p\) is false. Treating \(q\) as proof of \(p\) is the fallacy of affirming the consequent, so whether "it rains" is true remains undetermined.
questions.hint: Ask whether the consequent being true is the only possible way it could become true.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of the antecedent given the implication and consequent.
questions.question: Let \(p\): "It rains." and \(q\): "The outdoor concert is cancelled." The implication \(p \rightarrow q\) is true, and \(q\) is false. What must be the truth value of \(p\)?
questions.explanation: An implication \(p \rightarrow q\) is false only when \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false. Since \(p \rightarrow q\) is given as true, the combination \(p\)=True, \(q\)=False cannot occur. As \(q\) is false, \(p\) must therefore be False.
questions.hint: Recall the only row of the truth table where an implication is false, and rule it out.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the unique truth-value combination that makes an implication false.
questions.question: Let \(p\): "It rains." and \(q\): "The outdoor concert is cancelled." If the implication \(p \rightarrow q\) is false, what must be the truth values of \(p\) and \(q\)?
questions.explanation: An implication \(p \rightarrow q\) is false in exactly one case: when the antecedent \(p\) is True and the consequent \(q\) is False. This is the only row of the truth table producing a false implication.
questions.hint: There is exactly one row of the implication truth table that yields False — identify it.

questions.learningObjective: Form the converse of a given conditional statement.
questions.question: What is the converse of the statement "If it rains, then the outdoor concert is cancelled"?

options.label: A
options.text: If it does not rain, then the outdoor concert is not cancelled.

options.label: B
options.text: If the outdoor concert is not cancelled, then it does not rain.

options.label: C
options.text: If the outdoor concert is cancelled, then it rains.

questions.explanation: The converse of \(p \rightarrow q\) is formed by swapping the antecedent and consequent, giving \(q \rightarrow p\): "If the outdoor concert is cancelled, then it rains." This is different from the inverse (which negates both parts) and the contrapositive (which negates and swaps both parts).
questions.hint: The converse simply reverses the order of the original antecedent and consequent, without adding any negations.

questions.learningObjective: Form the inverse of a given conditional statement.
questions.question: What is the inverse of the statement "If it rains, then the outdoor concert is cancelled"?

options.label: A
options.text: If the outdoor concert is cancelled, then it rains.

options.label: B
options.text: If it does not rain, then the outdoor concert is not cancelled.

options.label: C
options.text: If the outdoor concert is not cancelled, then it does not rain.

questions.explanation: The inverse of \(p \rightarrow q\) negates both the antecedent and the consequent without swapping their order, giving \(\neg p \rightarrow \neg q\): "If it does not rain, then the outdoor concert is not cancelled." This differs from the converse (which swaps without negating) and the contrapositive (which negates and swaps).
questions.hint: The inverse keeps the original order but negates both parts of the statement.

questions.learningObjective: Form the contrapositive of a given conditional statement and recognize its equivalence to the original.
questions.question: What is the contrapositive of the statement "If it rains, then the outdoor concert is cancelled"?

options.label: A
options.text: If the outdoor concert is cancelled, then it rains.

options.label: B
options.text: If the outdoor concert is not cancelled, then it does not rain.

options.label: C
options.text: If it does not rain, then the outdoor concert is not cancelled.

questions.explanation: The contrapositive of \(p \rightarrow q\) both negates and swaps the antecedent and consequent, giving \(\neg q \rightarrow \neg p\): "If the outdoor concert is not cancelled, then it does not rain." The contrapositive is always logically equivalent to the original statement, unlike the converse or inverse.
questions.hint: The contrapositive both swaps and negates the two parts of the original statement — and it is logically equivalent to it.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the disjunctive form logically equivalent to a conditional statement.
questions.question: Which expression is logically equivalent to \(p \rightarrow q\)?
questions.explanation: By the material implication rule, \(p \rightarrow q\) is logically equivalent to \(\neg p \lor q\): the implication is false only when \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false, which matches exactly when \(\neg p \lor q\) is false. Checking all four rows of the truth table confirms the two expressions always agree.
questions.hint: Write out the truth table for both the implication and each candidate expression, and compare row by row.

questions.learningObjective: Apply De Morgan's law to negate a conjunction.
questions.question: Which expression is logically equivalent to \(\neg(p \land q)\)?
questions.explanation:
By De Morgan's law, the negation of a conjunction equals the disjunction of the negations: \(
eg(p \land q) \equiv

By De Morgan's law, the negation of a disjunction equals the conjunction of the negations: \(
eg(p \lor q) \equiv 
eg p \land 
eg q\). \(p \lor q\) is true whenever at least one of \(p\), \(q\) is true, so its negation requires both to be false simultaneously — which is exactly \(
eg p \land 
eg q\).
questions.hint: Negating an OR turns it into an AND of the negated parts.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the truth value of a biconditional given the truth values of its components.
questions.question: Suppose \(p\) is False and \(q\) is False. What is the truth value of \(p \leftrightarrow q\)?
questions.explanation: The biconditional \(p \leftrightarrow q\) is true exactly when \(p\) and \(q\) have the same truth value. Here \(p\) is False and \(q\) is False, so they match, making \(p \leftrightarrow q\) True.
questions.hint: A biconditional is true precisely when both sides agree — check whether the two values match here.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a conjunction given the truth values of its components.
questions.question: Given that \(p\) = False and \(q\) = False, evaluate \(p \land q\).
questions.explanation: A conjunction \(p \land q\) is true only when both \(p\) and \(q\) are true. Here \(p\) is False and \(q\) is False, so \(p \land q\) is False.
questions.hint: AND requires both parts to hold — check whether both values are true here.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a disjunction given the truth values of its components.
questions.question: If \(p\) is False and \(q\) is False, determine the truth value of \(p \lor q\).
questions.explanation: A disjunction \(p \lor q\) is true when at least one of \(p\), \(q\) is true. Here \(p\) is False and \(q\) is False, so \(p \lor q\) is False.
questions.hint: OR only needs one side to be true — check if at least one value holds here.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the negation of a proposition.
questions.question: Suppose \(p\) is False. What is the truth value of \(\neg p\)?
questions.explanation: Negation flips the truth value: since \(p\) is False, \(\neg p\) is True.
questions.hint: Negation simply reverses the truth value of the statement.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an exclusive-or expression given the truth values of its components.
questions.question: Suppose \(p\) is False and \(q\) is False. What is the truth value of \(p \oplus q\) (exclusive or)?
questions.explanation: Exclusive or (\(p \oplus q\)) is true exactly when \(p\) and \(q\) have different truth values. Here \(p\) is False and \(q\) is False, so they match, making \(p \oplus q\) False.
questions.hint: XOR is true only when exactly one of the two statements is true, not both and not neither.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a compound Boolean expression involving AND, OR, and NOT.
questions.question: Suppose \(p\) is False, \(q\) is False, and \(r\) is False. What is the truth value of \((p \land q) \lor \neg r\)?
questions.explanation: First evaluate \(p \land q\): since \(p\) is False and \(q\) is False, \(p \land q\) is False. Next, \(\neg r\) is True since \(r\) is False. Combining with OR: False \(\lor\) True = True.
questions.hint: Evaluate the parenthesized conjunction first, then the negation, and finally combine them with OR.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a compound Boolean expression involving negation, conjunction, and disjunction.
questions.question: Given that \(p\) = False, \(q\) = True, and \(r\) = True, evaluate \(\neg p \lor (q \land r)\).
questions.explanation: First evaluate \(q \land r\): since \(q\) is True and \(r\) is True, \(q \land r\) is True. Next, \(\neg p\) is True since \(p\) is False. Combining with OR: True \(\lor\) True = True.
questions.hint: Evaluate the parenthesized conjunction and the negation separately, then combine with OR.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish necessary from sufficient conditions in a numerical divisibility context.
questions.question: For a positive integer \(n\), being divisible by 3 is a ______ condition for \(n\) being divisible by 6.
questions.explanation: Every integer that is divisible by 6 is also divisible by 3 (since divisible by 6 implies divisible by 3), so being divisible by 3 is required whenever \(n\) is divisible by 6 — that makes it a necessary condition. However, being divisible by 3 alone does not guarantee \(n\) is divisible by 6, so it is not sufficient.
questions.hint: Test each implication between the two divisibility properties. Try a number that satisfies one property and check whether it must satisfy the other.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the antecedent of a true conditional as a sufficient condition for the consequent.
questions.question: Given the true statement "If the access code is valid, then the door unlocks," the condition "the access code is valid" is a ______ condition for "the door unlocks."
questions.explanation: In a true conditional statement, the antecedent being true is enough on its own to guarantee that the consequent is true — that is precisely what makes the antecedent ("the access code is valid") a sufficient condition for the consequent ("the door unlocks"). It is not necessarily a necessary condition, because "the door unlocks" could potentially be true for other reasons even when "the access code is valid" is false.
questions.hint: Ask: does the truth of the first statement alone guarantee the second? That describes sufficiency.

questions.learningObjective: Construct and interpret a truth table to count true outcomes of an expression.
questions.question: In the truth table for \(p \land q\) over all four combinations of \(p\) and \(q\), how many rows evaluate to True?
questions.explanation: Checking all four combinations of \(p\) and \(q\) (TT, TF, FT, FF) against \(p \land q\) shows it evaluates to True in exactly 1 of the 4 rows.
questions.hint: Systematically evaluate the expression for all four combinations of the two variables, then count the True results.

questions.learningObjective: Rewrite a conditional with a negated antecedent as an equivalent disjunction.
questions.question: Let \(p\): "A student passes the final exam." and \(q\): "A certificate is issued." Which expression is logically equivalent to "If a student does not pass the final exam, then a certificate is issued" (that is, \(\neg p \rightarrow q\))?
questions.explanation:
"If a student does not pass the final exam, then a certificate is issued" is \(
eg p ightarrow q\), which by the material implication rule is equivalent to \(
eg(
eg p) \lor q \equiv p \lor q\). So the statement is true whenever at least one of \(p\) or \(q\) holds.

questions.learningObjective: Combine a conditional statement with a confirmed premise to deduce a valid conclusion.
questions.question: All of the following are true: (1) If the invoice is paid in full, then the order is shipped. (2) The invoice is paid in full. Which of these statements must also be true?
questions.explanation: Statement (2) confirms the antecedent of the conditional in (1) is true. By modus ponens, since "the invoice is paid in full" is true and "If the invoice is paid in full, then the order is shipped" is true, the consequent "the order is shipped" must also be true.
questions.hint: Combine the two given facts using modus ponens: a true antecedent plus a true implication forces the consequent.

questions.learningObjective: Chain two conditional statements using hypothetical syllogism and apply modus ponens.
questions.question: Given: (1) If the number x is a multiple of 8, then the number x is a multiple of 4. (2) If the number x is a multiple of 4, then a certificate is issued. (3) The number x is a multiple of 8. What can be validly concluded?

options.label: B
options.text: No conclusion can be drawn about whether a certificate is issued.

questions.explanation: By hypothetical syllogism, statements (1) and (2) combine to give "If the number x is a multiple of 8, then a certificate is issued." Since (3) confirms "the number x is a multiple of 8" is true, modus ponens then gives us "a certificate is issued" as a valid conclusion.
questions.hint: First chain the two implications together, then apply the confirmed premise.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish genuinely equivalent rewrites of a conditional from the (non-equivalent) converse.
questions.question:
Three statements are proposed as equivalents of \(p ightarrow q\): \(
eg p \lor q\), \(
eg q ightarrow 
eg p\), and \(q ightarrow p\). Which one is NOT logically equivalent to \(p ightarrow q\)?
questions.explanation:
\(
eg p \lor q\) is the material-implication form of \(p ightarrow q\), and \(
eg q ightarrow 
eg p\) is its contrapositive — both are logically equivalent to \(p ightarrow q\). However, \(q ightarrow p\) is the converse, which is not generally equivalent (it can differ in truth value, e.g. when \(p\) is false and \(q\) is true).
questions.hint: Two of the three are standard equivalent rewrites of an implication; the third simply swaps antecedent and consequent.

questions.learningObjective: Correctly apply operator precedence (NOT, AND, OR) when evaluating a compound expression.
questions.question: Suppose \(p\) is True, \(q\) is False, and \(r\) is True. Using standard precedence (NOT before AND before OR), what is the truth value of \(\neg p \land q \lor r\)?
questions.explanation:
By precedence, \(
eg p \land q \lor r\) is parsed as \((
eg p \land q) \lor r\). First, \(
eg p\) = False. Then \(
eg p \land q\) = False \(\land\) False = False. Finally, False \(\lor\) True = True.
questions.hint: Apply NOT first, then AND, and only then OR — do not evaluate strictly left to right.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a conjunction of two number-property propositions.
questions.question: Let \(p\): "12 is a multiple of 4." and \(q\): "12 is a multiple of 3." What is the truth value of \(p \land q\)?

options.label: C
options.text: Cannot be determined without a calculator

questions.explanation: Check each part: 12 \(\div\) 4 is exact, so \(p\) is True. 12 \(\div\) 3 is exact, so \(q\) is True. Since \(p \land q\) requires both to be true, \(p \land q\) is True.
questions.hint: Check divisibility by 4 and by 3 separately before combining the results with AND.

questions.hint: AND requires both parts to hold — check whether both values are true here.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a disjunction given the truth values of its components.
questions.question: Suppose \(a\) is False and \(b\) is True. What is the truth value of \(a \lor b\)?
questions.explanation: A disjunction \(a \lor b\) is true when at least one of \(a\), \(b\) is true. Here \(a\) is False and \(b\) is True, so \(a \lor b\) is True.
questions.hint: OR only needs one side to be true — check if at least one value holds here.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the negation of a proposition.
questions.question: Suppose \(a\) is False. What is the truth value of \(\neg a\)?
questions.explanation: Negation flips the truth value: since \(a\) is False, \(\neg a\) is True.
questions.hint: Negation simply reverses the truth value of the statement.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an exclusive-or expression given the truth values of its components.
questions.question: Given that \(a\) = False and \(b\) = True, evaluate \(a \oplus b\) (exclusive or).
questions.explanation: Exclusive or (\(a \oplus b\)) is true exactly when \(a\) and \(b\) have different truth values. Here \(a\) is False and \(b\) is True, so they differ, making \(a \oplus b\) True.
questions.hint: XOR is true only when exactly one of the two statements is true, not both and not neither.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a compound Boolean expression involving AND, OR, and NOT.
questions.question: Given that \(a\) = False, \(b\) = False, and \(c\) = True, evaluate \((a \land b) \lor \neg c\).
questions.explanation: First evaluate \(a \land b\): since \(a\) is False and \(b\) is False, \(a \land b\) is False. Next, \(\neg c\) is False since \(c\) is True. Combining with OR: False \(\lor\) False = False.
questions.hint: Evaluate the parenthesized conjunction first, then the negation, and finally combine them with OR.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a compound Boolean expression involving negation, conjunction, and disjunction.
questions.question: If \(a\) is True, \(b\) is False, and \(c\) is False, determine the truth value of \(\neg a \lor (b \land c)\).
questions.explanation: First evaluate \(b \land c\): since \(b\) is False and \(c\) is False, \(b \land c\) is False. Next, \(\neg a\) is False since \(a\) is True. Combining with OR: False \(\lor\) False = False.
questions.hint: Evaluate the parenthesized conjunction and the negation separately, then combine with OR.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish necessary from sufficient conditions in a numerical divisibility context.
questions.question: For a positive integer \(n\), being divisible by 2 is a ______ condition for \(n\) being divisible by 8.
questions.explanation: Every integer that is divisible by 8 is also divisible by 2 (since divisible by 8 implies divisible by 2), so being divisible by 2 is required whenever \(n\) is divisible by 8 — that makes it a necessary condition. However, being divisible by 2 alone does not guarantee \(n\) is divisible by 8, so it is not sufficient.
questions.hint: Test each implication between the two divisibility properties. Try a number that satisfies one property and check whether it must satisfy the other.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the antecedent of a true conditional as a sufficient condition for the consequent.
questions.question: Given the true statement "If the battery is fully charged, then the phone powers on," the condition "the battery is fully charged" is a ______ condition for "the phone powers on."
questions.explanation: In a true conditional statement, the antecedent being true is enough on its own to guarantee that the consequent is true — that is precisely what makes the antecedent ("the battery is fully charged") a sufficient condition for the consequent ("the phone powers on"). It is not necessarily a necessary condition, because "the phone powers on" could potentially be true for other reasons even when "the battery is fully charged" is false.
questions.hint: Ask: does the truth of the first statement alone guarantee the second? That describes sufficiency.

questions.learningObjective: Apply modus ponens to draw valid conclusions from a true conditional statement.

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing can be concluded from the given information.

options.label: C
options.text: The number n is divisible by 3.

questions.explanation: This is an application of modus ponens: if \(p \rightarrow q\) is true and \(p\) is true, then \(q\) must be true. Since the conditional holds and the antecedent ("the number n is divisible by 6") is true, the consequent ("the number n is divisible by 3") must also be true.
questions.hint: Think about what modus ponens allows you to conclude when both the implication and its antecedent are true.

questions.question: The conditional "If the number n is divisible by 6, then the number n is divisible by 3" is true. Suppose it is observed that the number n is not divisible by 3. What can be validly concluded?

options.text: The number n is divisible by 6.

options.label: B

options.text: The number n is not divisible by 6.

questions.hint: Check whether the implication makes any promise about the consequent when the antecedent is false.

options.label: B
options.text: If the number n is not divisible by 3, then the number n is not divisible by 6.

options.label: C
options.text: If the number n is divisible by 3, then the number n is divisible by 6.

questions.explanation: The converse of \(p \rightarrow q\) is formed by swapping the antecedent and consequent, giving \(q \rightarrow p\): "If the number n is divisible by 3, then the number n is divisible by 6." This is different from the inverse (which negates both parts) and the contrapositive (which negates and swaps both parts).
questions.hint: The converse simply reverses the order of the original antecedent and consequent, without adding any negations.

options.label: B
options.text: If the number n is not divisible by 3, then the number n is not divisible by 6.

options.label: C
options.text: If the number n is not divisible by 6, then the number n is not divisible by 3.

This differs from the converse (which swaps without negating) and the contrapositive (which negates and swaps).
questions.hint: The inverse keeps the original order but negates both parts of the statement.

options.text: If the number n is not divisible by 3, then the number n is not divisible by 6.

options.label: C

questions.learningObjective: Apply modus ponens to draw valid conclusions from a true conditional statement.
questions.question: Consider the statement: "If the traffic light is red, then the cars must stop." This conditional is known to be true, and it is also known that the traffic light is red. What can be validly concluded?

options.label: A
options.text: The traffic light is not red.

options.label: C
options.text: Nothing can be concluded from the given information.

questions.explanation: This is an application of modus ponens: if \(p \rightarrow q\) is true and \(p\) is true, then \(q\) must be true. Since the conditional holds and the antecedent ("the traffic light is red") is true, the consequent ("the cars must stop") must also be true.
questions.hint: Think about what modus ponens allows you to conclude when both the implication and its antecedent are true.

questions.learningObjective: Apply modus tollens to draw valid conclusions from a true conditional statement.
questions.question: The conditional "If the traffic light is red, then the cars must stop" is true. Suppose it is observed that the cars do not have to stop. What can be validly concluded?

options.label: B
options.text: The traffic light is not red.

options.label: C
options.text: No valid conclusion can be drawn about whether the traffic light is red.

questions.explanation: This is modus tollens: if \(p \rightarrow q\) is true and \(q\) is false, then \(p\) must be false. Since \(q\) ("the cars must stop") is false (that is, "the cars do not have to stop"), \(p\) ("the traffic light is red") cannot be true, so it must be false — that is, "the traffic light is not red."
questions.hint: Recall that a true implication is only violated when the antecedent is true and the consequent is false — use this to reason backward.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize that denying the antecedent does not yield a valid conclusion.
questions.question: The conditional "If the traffic light is red, then the cars must stop" is true. It is observed that the traffic light is not red. What can be validly concluded about whether the cars must stop?

options.label: A
options.text: It cannot be determined whether the cars must stop.

options.label: B
options.text: The cars do not have to stop.

questions.explanation: A conditional \(p \rightarrow q\) says nothing about what happens when \(p\) is false; \(q\) may be true or false. Concluding that \(q\) is false from \(\neg p\) is the fallacy of denying the antecedent. Since "the traffic light is not red" (the antecedent is false), the truth of "the cars must stop" is left undetermined by this conditional alone.
questions.hint: Check whether the implication makes any promise about the consequent when the antecedent is false.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize that affirming the consequent does not yield a valid conclusion.
questions.question: The conditional "If the traffic light is red, then the cars must stop" is true. It is observed that the cars must stop. What can be validly concluded about whether the traffic light is red?

options.label: B
options.text: The traffic light is not red.

options.label: C
options.text: It cannot be determined whether the traffic light is red.

questions.explanation: Knowing \(q\) is true does not let us conclude \(p\) is true, since \(p \rightarrow q\) allows \(q\) to be true even when \(p\) is false. Treating \(q\) as proof of \(p\) is the fallacy of affirming the consequent, so whether "the traffic light is red" is true remains undetermined.
questions.hint: Ask whether the consequent being true is the only possible way it could become true.

eg(c \land d) \equiv 
eg c \lor

Checking all four rows of the truth table confirms the two expressions always agree.
questions.hint: Write out the truth table for both the implication and each candidate expression, and compare row by row.

questions.learningObjective: Apply De Morgan's law to negate a conjunction.
questions.question: Which expression is logically equivalent to \(\neg(j \land k)\)?

By De Morgan's law, the negation of a conjunction equals the disjunction of the negations: \(
eg(j \land k) \equiv 
eg j \lor

questions.learningObjective: Apply De Morgan's law to negate a disjunction.
questions.question: Which expression is logically equivalent to \(\neg(j \lor k)\)?
questions.explanation:
By De Morgan's law, the negation of a disjunction equals the conjunction of the negations: \(
eg(j \lor k) \equiv 
eg j \land 
eg k\). \(j \lor k\) is true whenever at least one of \(j\), \(k\) is true, so its negation requires both to be false simultaneously — which is exactly \(
eg j \land 
eg k\).
questions.hint: Negating an OR turns it into an AND of the negated parts.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the truth value of a biconditional given the truth values of its components.
questions.question: Given that \(j\) = True and \(k\) = True, evaluate \(j \leftrightarrow k\).
questions.explanation: The biconditional \(j \leftrightarrow k\) is true exactly when \(j\) and \(k\) have the same truth value. Here \(j\) is True and \(k\) is True, so they match, making \(j \leftrightarrow k\) True.
questions.hint: A biconditional is true precisely when both sides agree — check whether the two values match here.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a conjunction given the truth values of its components.
questions.question: If \(j\) is True and \(k\) is True, determine the truth value of \(j \land k\).
questions.explanation: A conjunction \(j \land k\) is true only when both \(j\) and \(k\) are true. Here \(j\) is True and \(k\) is True, so \(j \land k\) is True.
questions.hint: AND requires both parts to hold — check whether both values are true here.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a disjunction given the truth values of its components.
questions.question: Suppose \(j\) is True and \(k\) is True. What is the truth value of \(j \lor k\)?
questions.explanation: A disjunction \(j \lor k\) is true when at least one of \(j\), \(k\) is true. Here \(j\) is True and \(k\) is True, so \(j \lor k\) is True.
questions.hint: OR only needs one side to be true — check if at least one value holds here.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the negation of a proposition.
questions.question: Suppose \(j\) is True. What is the truth value of \(\neg j\)?

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an exclusive-or expression given the truth values of its components.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a compound Boolean expression involving AND, OR, and NOT.
questions.question: Given that \(u\) = True, \(v\) = True, and \(w\) = True, evaluate \((u \land v) \lor \neg w\).
questions.explanation: First evaluate \(u \land v\): since \(u\) is True and \(v\) is True, \(u \land v\) is True. Next, \(\neg w\) is False since \(w\) is True. Combining with OR: True \(\lor\) False = True.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish necessary from sufficient conditions in a numerical divisibility context.
questions.question: For a positive integer \(n\), being a multiple of 7 is a ______ condition for \(n\) being a multiple of 14.
questions.explanation: Every integer that is a multiple of 14 is also a multiple of 7 (since a multiple of 14 implies a multiple of 7), so being a multiple of 7 is required whenever \(n\) is a multiple of 14 — that makes it a necessary condition. However, being a multiple of 7 alone does not guarantee \(n\) is a multiple of 14, so it is not sufficient.
questions.hint: Test each implication between the two divisibility properties. Try a number that satisfies one property and check whether it must satisfy the other.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the antecedent of a true conditional as a sufficient condition for the consequent.

questions.explanation: In a true conditional statement, the antecedent being true is enough on its own to guarantee that the consequent is true — that is precisely what makes the antecedent ("the flight departs late") a sufficient condition for the consequent ("passengers miss their connection"). It is not necessarily a necessary condition, because "passengers miss their connection" could potentially be true for other reasons even when "the flight departs late" is false.
questions.hint: Ask: does the truth of the first statement alone guarantee the second? That describes sufficiency.

options.label: A
options.text: The number n is not even.

options.label: B
options.text: No conclusion can be drawn about whether the number n is even.

questions.explanation: By hypothetical syllogism, statements (1) and (2) combine to give "If the password entered is correct, then the number n is even." Since (3) confirms "the password entered is correct" is true, modus ponens then gives us "the number n is even" as a valid conclusion.
questions.hint: First chain the two implications together, then apply the confirmed premise.

questions.learningObjective: Apply modus ponens to draw valid conclusions from a true conditional statement.
questions.question: Consider the statement: "If the temperature drops below 0°C, then the water freezes." This conditional is known to be true, and it is also known that the temperature drops below 0°C. What can be validly concluded?

options.label: A
options.text: The temperature does not drop below 0°C.

options.label: C
options.text: Nothing can be concluded from the given information.

questions.explanation: This is an application of modus ponens: if \(p \rightarrow q\) is true and \(p\) is true, then \(q\) must be true. Since the conditional holds and the antecedent ("the temperature drops below 0°C") is true, the consequent ("the water freezes") must also be true.
questions.hint: Think about what modus ponens allows you to conclude when both the implication and its antecedent are true.

questions.learningObjective: Apply modus tollens to draw valid conclusions from a true conditional statement.

options.label: B
options.text: The temperature does not drop below 0°C.

options.label: C
options.text: No valid conclusion can be drawn about whether the temperature drops below 0°C.

questions.explanation: This is modus tollens: if \(p \rightarrow q\) is true and \(q\) is false, then \(p\) must be false. Since \(q\) ("the water freezes") is false (that is, "the water does not freeze"), \(p\) ("the temperature drops below 0°C") cannot be true, so it must be false — that is, "the temperature does not drop below 0°C."
questions.hint: Recall that a true implication is only violated when the antecedent is true and the consequent is false — use this to reason backward.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize that denying the antecedent does not yield a valid conclusion.
questions.question: The conditional "If the temperature drops below 0°C, then the water freezes" is true. It is observed that the temperature does not drop below 0°C. What can be validly concluded about whether the water freezes?

options.label: C
options.text: It cannot be determined whether the water freezes.

questions.explanation: A conditional \(p \rightarrow q\) says nothing about what happens when \(p\) is false; \(q\) may be true or false. Concluding that \(q\) is false from \(\neg p\) is the fallacy of denying the antecedent. Since "the temperature does not drop below 0°C" (the antecedent is false), the truth of "the water freezes" is left undetermined by this conditional alone.
questions.hint: Check whether the implication makes any promise about the consequent when the antecedent is false.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize that affirming the consequent does not yield a valid conclusion.

options.label: B
options.text: It cannot be determined whether the temperature drops below 0°C.

options.label: C
options.text: The temperature does not drop below 0°C.

questions.explanation: Knowing \(q\) is true does not let us conclude \(p\) is true, since \(p \rightarrow q\) allows \(q\) to be true even when \(p\) is false. Treating \(q\) as proof of \(p\) is the fallacy of affirming the consequent, so whether "the temperature drops below 0°C" is true remains undetermined.
questions.hint: Ask whether the consequent being true is the only possible way it could become true.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of the antecedent given the implication and consequent.
questions.question: Let \(e\): "The temperature drops below 0°C." and \(f\): "The water freezes." The implication \(e \rightarrow f\) is true, and \(f\) is false. What must be the truth value of \(e\)?
questions.explanation: An implication \(e \rightarrow f\) is false only when \(e\) is true and \(f\) is false. Since \(e \rightarrow f\) is given as true, the combination \(e\)=True, \(f\)=False cannot occur. As \(f\) is false, \(e\) must therefore be False.
questions.hint: Recall the only row of the truth table where an implication is false, and rule it out.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the unique truth-value combination that makes an implication false.

questions.explanation: An implication \(e \rightarrow f\) is false in exactly one case: when the antecedent \(e\) is True and the consequent \(f\) is False. This is the only row of the truth table producing a false implication.
questions.hint: There is exactly one row of the implication truth table that yields False — identify it.

questions.learningObjective: Form the converse of a given conditional statement.
questions.question: What is the converse of the statement "If the temperature drops below 0°C, then the water freezes"?

options.label: A
options.text: If the temperature does not drop below 0°C, then the water does not freeze.

options.label: B
options.text: If the water does not freeze, then the temperature does not drop below 0°C.

options.label: C
options.text: If the water freezes, then the temperature drops below 0°C.

questions.explanation: The converse of \(p \rightarrow q\) is formed by swapping the antecedent and consequent, giving \(q \rightarrow p\): "If the water freezes, then the temperature drops below 0°C." This is different from the inverse (which negates both parts) and the contrapositive (which negates and swaps both parts).
questions.hint: The converse simply reverses the order of the original antecedent and consequent, without adding any negations.

questions.learningObjective: Form the inverse of a given conditional statement.
questions.question: What is the inverse of the statement "If the temperature drops below 0°C, then the water freezes"?

options.label: A
options.text: If the temperature does not drop below 0°C, then the water does not freeze.

options.label: B
options.text: If the water freezes, then the temperature drops below 0°C.

options.label: C
options.text: If the water does not freeze, then the temperature does not drop below 0°C.

questions.explanation: The inverse of \(p \rightarrow q\) negates both the antecedent and the consequent without swapping their order, giving \(\neg p \rightarrow \neg q\): "If the temperature does not drop below 0°C, then the water does not freeze." This differs from the converse (which swaps without negating) and the contrapositive (which negates and swaps).
questions.hint: The inverse keeps the original order but negates both parts of the statement.

questions.learningObjective: Form the contrapositive of a given conditional statement and recognize its equivalence to the original.
questions.question: What is the contrapositive of the statement "If the temperature drops below 0°C, then the water freezes"?

options.label: A
options.text: If the water does not freeze, then the temperature does not drop below 0°C.

options.label: B
options.text: If the water freezes, then the temperature drops below 0°C.

options.label: C
options.text: If the temperature does not drop below 0°C, then the water does not freeze.

questions.explanation: The contrapositive of \(p \rightarrow q\) both negates and swaps the antecedent and consequent, giving \(\neg q \rightarrow \neg p\): "If the water does not freeze, then the temperature does not drop below 0°C." The contrapositive is always logically equivalent to the original statement, unlike the converse or inverse.
questions.hint: The contrapositive both swaps and negates the two parts of the original statement — and it is logically equivalent to it.

questions.learningObjective: Chain two conditional statements using hypothetical syllogism and apply modus ponens.
questions.question: Given: (1) If the switch is turned on, then the circuit is closed. (2) If the circuit is closed, then a distinction is awarded. (3) The switch is turned on. What can be validly concluded?

options.label: C
options.text: No conclusion can be drawn about whether a distinction is awarded.

questions.explanation: By hypothetical syllogism, statements (1) and (2) combine to give "If the switch is turned on, then a distinction is awarded." Since (3) confirms "the switch is turned on" is true, modus ponens then gives us "a distinction is awarded" as a valid conclusion.
questions.hint: First chain the two implications together, then apply the confirmed premise.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish genuinely equivalent rewrites of a conditional from the (non-equivalent) converse.
questions.question:
Three statements are proposed as equivalents of \(e ightarrow f\): \(
eg e \lor f\), \(
eg f ightarrow 
eg e\), and \(f ightarrow e\). Which one is NOT logically equivalent to \(e ightarrow f\)?
questions.explanation:
\(
eg e \lor f\) is the material-implication form of \(e ightarrow f\), and \(
eg f ightarrow 
eg e\) is its contrapositive — both are logically equivalent to \(e ightarrow f\). However, \(f ightarrow e\) is the converse, which is not generally equivalent (it can differ in truth value, e.g. when \(e\) is false and \(f\) is true).
questions.hint: Two of the three are standard equivalent rewrites of an implication; the third simply swaps antecedent and consequent.

questions.learningObjective: Correctly apply operator precedence (NOT, AND, OR) when evaluating a compound expression.
questions.question: Suppose \(l\) is True, \(m\) is False, and \(n\) is True. Using standard precedence (NOT before AND before OR), what is the truth value of \(\neg l \land m \lor n\)?
questions.explanation:
By precedence, \(
eg l \land m \lor n\) is parsed as \((
eg l \land m) \lor n\). First, \(
eg l\) = False. Then \(
eg l \land m\) = False \(\land\) False = False. Finally, False \(\lor\) True = True.
questions.hint: Apply NOT first, then AND, and only then OR — do not evaluate strictly left to right.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a conjunction of two number-property propositions.
questions.question: Let \(p\): "48 is a multiple of 4." and \(q\): "48 is a multiple of 3." What is the truth value of \(p \land q\)?

options.label: C
options.text: Cannot be determined without a calculator

questions.explanation: Check each part: 48 \(\div\) 4 is exact, so \(p\) is True. 48 \(\div\) 3 is exact, so \(q\) is True. Since \(p \land q\) requires both to be true, \(p \land q\) is True.
questions.hint: Check divisibility by 4 and by 3 separately before combining the results with AND.

questions.learningObjective: Apply modus ponens to draw valid conclusions from a true conditional statement.
questions.question: Consider the statement: "If the file is saved, then the changes persist after closing." This conditional is known to be true, and it is also known that the file is saved. What can be validly concluded?

options.label: C
options.text: Nothing can be concluded from the given information.

questions.explanation: This is an application of modus ponens: if \(p \rightarrow q\) is true and \(p\) is true, then \(q\) must be true. Since the conditional holds and the antecedent ("the file is saved") is true, the consequent ("the changes persist after closing") must also be true.
questions.hint: Think about what modus ponens allows you to conclude when both the implication and its antecedent are true.

questions.learningObjective: Apply modus tollens to draw valid conclusions from a true conditional statement.
questions.question: The conditional "If the file is saved, then the changes persist after closing" is true. Suppose it is observed that the changes do not persist after closing. What can be validly concluded?

options.label: C
options.text: No valid conclusion can be drawn about whether the file is saved.

questions.explanation: This is modus tollens: if \(p \rightarrow q\) is true and \(q\) is false, then \(p\) must be false. Since \(q\) ("the changes persist after closing") is false (that is, "the changes do not persist after closing"), \(p\) ("the file is saved") cannot be true, so it must be false — that is, "the file is not saved."
questions.hint: Recall that a true implication is only violated when the antecedent is true and the consequent is false — use this to reason backward.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize that denying the antecedent does not yield a valid conclusion.
questions.question: The conditional "If the file is saved, then the changes persist after closing" is true. It is observed that the file is not saved. What can be validly concluded about whether the changes persist after closing?

options.label: A
options.text: The changes do not persist after closing.

options.label: B
options.text: It cannot be determined whether the changes persist after closing.

questions.explanation: A conditional \(p \rightarrow q\) says nothing about what happens when \(p\) is false; \(q\) may be true or false. Concluding that \(q\) is false from \(\neg p\) is the fallacy of denying the antecedent. Since "the file is not saved" (the antecedent is false), the truth of "the changes persist after closing" is left undetermined by this conditional alone.
questions.hint: Check whether the implication makes any promise about the consequent when the antecedent is false.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize that affirming the consequent does not yield a valid conclusion.
questions.question: The conditional "If the file is saved, then the changes persist after closing" is true. It is observed that the changes persist after closing. What can be validly concluded about whether the file is saved?

options.label: A
options.text: It cannot be determined whether the file is saved.

questions.explanation: Knowing \(q\) is true does not let us conclude \(p\) is true, since \(p \rightarrow q\) allows \(q\) to be true even when \(p\) is false. Treating \(q\) as proof of \(p\) is the fallacy of affirming the consequent, so whether "the file is saved" is true remains undetermined.
questions.hint: Ask whether the consequent being true is the only possible way it could become true.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of the antecedent given the implication and consequent.
questions.question: Let \(g\): "The file is saved." and \(h\): "The changes persist after closing." The implication \(g \rightarrow h\) is true, and \(h\) is false. What must be the truth value of \(g\)?
questions.explanation: An implication \(g \rightarrow h\) is false only when \(g\) is true and \(h\) is false. Since \(g \rightarrow h\) is given as true, the combination \(g\)=True, \(h\)=False cannot occur. As \(h\) is false, \(g\) must therefore be False.
questions.hint: Recall the only row of the truth table where an implication is false, and rule it out.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the unique truth-value combination that makes an implication false.
questions.question: Let \(g\): "The file is saved." and \(h\): "The changes persist after closing." If the implication \(g \rightarrow h\) is false, what must be the truth values of \(g\) and \(h\)?
questions.explanation: An implication \(g \rightarrow h\) is false in exactly one case: when the antecedent \(g\) is True and the consequent \(h\) is False. This is the only row of the truth table producing a false implication.
questions.hint: There is exactly one row of the implication truth table that yields False — identify it.

questions.learningObjective: Form the converse of a given conditional statement.
questions.question: What is the converse of the statement "If the file is saved, then the changes persist after closing"?

options.label: A
options.text: If the file is not saved, then the changes do not persist after closing.

options.label: B
options.text: If the changes do not persist after closing, then the file is not saved.

options.label: C
options.text: If the changes persist after closing, then the file is saved.

questions.explanation: The converse of \(p \rightarrow q\) is formed by swapping the antecedent and consequent, giving \(q \rightarrow p\): "If the changes persist after closing, then the file is saved." This is different from the inverse (which negates both parts) and the contrapositive (which negates and swaps both parts).
questions.hint: The converse simply reverses the order of the original antecedent and consequent, without adding any negations.

questions.learningObjective: Form the inverse of a given conditional statement.
questions.question: What is the inverse of the statement "If the file is saved, then the changes persist after closing"?

options.label: A
options.text: If the file is not saved, then the changes do not persist after closing.

options.label: B
options.text: If the changes persist after closing, then the file is saved.

options.label: C
options.text: If the changes do not persist after closing, then the file is not saved.

questions.explanation: The inverse of \(p \rightarrow q\) negates both the antecedent and the consequent without swapping their order, giving \(\neg p \rightarrow \neg q\): "If the file is not saved, then the changes do not persist after closing." This differs from the converse (which swaps without negating) and the contrapositive (which negates and swaps).
questions.hint: The inverse keeps the original order but negates both parts of the statement.

questions.learningObjective: Form the contrapositive of a given conditional statement and recognize its equivalence to the original.
questions.question: What is the contrapositive of the statement "If the file is saved, then the changes persist after closing"?

options.label: A
options.text: If the changes persist after closing, then the file is saved.

options.label: B
options.text: If the changes do not persist after closing, then the file is not saved.

options.label: C
options.text: If the file is not saved, then the changes do not persist after closing.

questions.explanation: The contrapositive of \(p \rightarrow q\) both negates and swaps the antecedent and consequent, giving \(\neg q \rightarrow \neg p\): "If the changes do not persist after closing, then the file is not saved." The contrapositive is always logically equivalent to the original statement, unlike the converse or inverse.
questions.hint: The contrapositive both swaps and negates the two parts of the original statement — and it is logically equivalent to it.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the disjunctive form logically equivalent to a conditional statement.
questions.question: Which expression is logically equivalent to \(g \rightarrow h\)?
questions.explanation: By the material implication rule, \(g \rightarrow h\) is logically equivalent to \(\neg g \lor h\): the implication is false only when \(g\) is true and \(h\) is false, which matches exactly when \(\neg g \lor h\) is false. Checking all four rows of the truth table confirms the two expressions always agree.
questions.hint: Write out the truth table for both the implication and each candidate expression, and compare row by row.

questions.learningObjective: Derive the correct negation of a conditional statement.
questions.question: Which expression is logically equivalent to the negation \(\neg(g \rightarrow h)\)?
questions.explanation:
Since \(g ightarrow h \equiv 
eg g \lor h\), negating both sides gives \(
eg(
eg g \lor h) \equiv g \land 
eg h\) by De Morgan's law. So the implication is false exactly when \(g\) is true and \(h\) is false, confirming \(
eg(g ightarrow h) \equiv g \land 
eg h\).
questions.hint: Rewrite the implication as a disjunction first, then apply De Morgan's law to negate it.

questions.learningObjective: Apply De Morgan's law to negate a conjunction.
questions.question: Which expression is logically equivalent to \(\neg(g \land h)\)?
questions.explanation:
By De Morgan's law, the negation of a conjunction equals the disjunction of the negations: \(
eg(g \land h) \equiv 
eg g \lor 
eg h\). \(g \land h\) is true only when both \(g\) and \(h\) are true, so its negation is true whenever at least one of \(g\), \(h\) is false — exactly what \(
eg g \lor 
eg h\) captures.
questions.hint: Negating an AND turns it into an OR of the negated parts — remember which connective flips into which.

questions.learningObjective: Apply De Morgan's law to negate a disjunction.
questions.question: Which expression is logically equivalent to \(\neg(g \lor h)\)?
questions.explanation:
By De Morgan's law, the negation of a disjunction equals the conjunction of the negations: \(
eg(g \lor h) \equiv 
eg g \land 
eg h\). \(g \lor h\) is true whenever at least one of \(g\), \(h\) is true, so its negation requires both to be false simultaneously — which is exactly \(
eg g \land 
eg h\).
questions.hint: Negating an OR turns it into an AND of the negated parts.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the truth value of a biconditional given the truth values of its components.
questions.question: Suppose \(g\) is False and \(h\) is True. What is the truth value of \(g \leftrightarrow h\)?
questions.explanation: The biconditional \(g \leftrightarrow h\) is true exactly when \(g\) and \(h\) have the same truth value. Here \(g\) is False and \(h\) is True, so they do not match, making \(g \leftrightarrow h\) False.
questions.hint: A biconditional is true precisely when both sides agree — check whether the two values match here.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a conjunction given the truth values of its components.
questions.question: Given that \(g\) = False and \(h\) = True, evaluate \(g \land h\).
questions.explanation: A conjunction \(g \land h\) is true only when both \(g\) and \(h\) are true. Here \(g\) is False and \(h\) is True, so \(g \land h\) is False.
questions.hint: AND requires both parts to hold — check whether both values are true here.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a disjunction given the truth values of its components.
questions.question: If \(g\) is False and \(h\) is True, determine the truth value of \(g \lor h\).
questions.explanation: A disjunction \(g \lor h\) is true when at least one of \(g\), \(h\) is true. Here \(g\) is False and \(h\) is True, so \(g \lor h\) is True.
questions.hint: OR only needs one side to be true — check if at least one value holds here.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the negation of a proposition.
questions.question: Suppose \(g\) is False. What is the truth value of \(\neg g\)?
questions.explanation: Negation flips the truth value: since \(g\) is False, \(\neg g\) is True.
questions.hint: Negation simply reverses the truth value of the statement.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an exclusive-or expression given the truth values of its components.
questions.question: Suppose \(g\) is False and \(h\) is True. What is the truth value of \(g \oplus h\) (exclusive or)?
questions.explanation: Exclusive or (\(g \oplus h\)) is true exactly when \(g\) and \(h\) have different truth values. Here \(g\) is False and \(h\) is True, so they differ, making \(g \oplus h\) True.
questions.hint: XOR is true only when exactly one of the two statements is true, not both and not neither.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a compound Boolean expression involving AND, OR, and NOT.
questions.question: Suppose \(y\) is False, \(z\) is False, and \(w\) is True. What is the truth value of \((y \land z) \lor \neg w\)?
questions.explanation: First evaluate \(y \land z\): since \(y\) is False and \(z\) is False, \(y \land z\) is False. Next, \(\neg w\) is False since \(w\) is True. Combining with OR: False \(\lor\) False = False.
questions.hint: Evaluate the parenthesized conjunction first, then the negation, and finally combine them with OR.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a compound Boolean expression involving negation, conjunction, and disjunction.
questions.question: Given that \(y\) = True, \(z\) = False, and \(w\) = False, evaluate \(\neg y \lor (z \land w)\).
questions.explanation: First evaluate \(z \land w\): since \(z\) is False and \(w\) is False, \(z \land w\) is False. Next, \(\neg y\) is False since \(y\) is True. Combining with OR: False \(\lor\) False = False.
questions.hint: Evaluate the parenthesized conjunction and the negation separately, then combine with OR.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish necessary from sufficient conditions in a numerical divisibility context.
questions.question: For a positive integer \(n\), being divisible by 5 is a ______ condition for \(n\) being divisible by 25.
questions.explanation: Every integer that is divisible by 25 is also divisible by 5 (since divisible by 25 implies divisible by 5), so being divisible by 5 is required whenever \(n\) is divisible by 25 — that makes it a necessary condition. However, being divisible by 5 alone does not guarantee \(n\) is divisible by 25, so it is not sufficient.
questions.hint: Test each implication between the two divisibility properties. Try a number that satisfies one property and check whether it must satisfy the other.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the antecedent of a true conditional as a sufficient condition for the consequent.
questions.question: Given the true statement "If the password entered is correct, then the account is unlocked," the condition "the password entered is correct" is a ______ condition for "the account is unlocked."
questions.explanation: In a true conditional statement, the antecedent being true is enough on its own to guarantee that the consequent is true — that is precisely what makes the antecedent ("the password entered is correct") a sufficient condition for the consequent ("the account is unlocked"). It is not necessarily a necessary condition, because "the account is unlocked" could potentially be true for other reasons even when "the password entered is correct" is false.
questions.hint: Ask: does the truth of the first statement alone guarantee the second? That describes sufficiency.

questions.learningObjective: Construct and interpret a truth table to count true outcomes of an expression.
questions.question: In the truth table for \(g \lor h\) over all four combinations of \(g\) and \(h\), how many rows evaluate to True?
questions.explanation: Checking all four combinations of \(g\) and \(h\) (TT, TF, FT, FF) against \(g \lor h\) shows it evaluates to True in exactly 3 of the 4 rows.
questions.hint: Systematically evaluate the expression for all four combinations of the two variables, then count the True results.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the law of double negation to simplify an expression.
questions.question: Which expression is logically equivalent to \(\neg \neg g\)?

options.label: C

The law of double negation states that negating a proposition twice restores its original truth value: \(
eg 
eg g \equiv g\). If \(g\) is true, \(
eg g\) is false, and \(
eg 
eg g\) is true again — matching \(g\).
questions.hint: Apply negation twice to a single true or false value and see where you end up.

questions.learningObjective: Rewrite a conditional with a negated antecedent as an equivalent disjunction.
questions.question: Let \(p\): "The tank pressure exceeds the limit." and \(q\): "The safety valve opens." Which expression is logically equivalent to "If the tank pressure does not exceed the limit, then the safety valve opens" (that is, \(\neg p \rightarrow q\))?
questions.explanation:
"If the tank pressure does not exceed the limit, then the safety valve opens" is \(
eg p ightarrow q\), which by the material implication rule is equivalent to \(
eg(
eg p) \lor q \equiv p \lor q\). So the statement is true whenever at least one of \(p\) or \(q\) holds.
questions.hint: Rewrite the implication as "not antecedent or consequent," then simplify the double negation.

questions.question: All of the following are true: (1) If the patient's temperature exceeds 38°C, then a fever is recorded. (2) The patient's temperature exceeds 38°C. Which of these statements must also be true?
questions.explanation: Statement (2) confirms the antecedent of the conditional in (1) is true. By modus ponens, since "the patient's temperature exceeds 38°C" is true and "If the patient's temperature exceeds 38°C, then a fever is recorded" is true, the consequent "a fever is recorded" must also be true.
questions.hint: Combine the two given facts using modus ponens: a true antecedent plus a true implication forces the consequent.

questions.question: Given: (1) If the number n is divisible by 4, then the number n is even. (2) If the number n is even, then the safety valve opens. (3) The number n is divisible by 4. What can be validly concluded?
